Case presented by Dr. Deyin Xing, MD, PhD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This is a 40 year old female with a right ovarian mass. Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.histology: This benign and rare tumor is a solid pseudopapillary neoplasm typically confined to the ovary and resembling its pancreatic counterpart. These tumors show an admixture of three primary histologic patterns: solid, nests, and pseudopapillae. In this case, the solid component is punctuated by cysts. Nests of cells are separated by hyalinized stroma and the pseudopapillae appear to have hyalinized cores. There are frequent intracytoplasmic and extracytoplasmic eosinophilic hyaline globules. On higher power, the cytology shows polygonal cells with eosinophilic to pale and foamy cytoplasm with paranuclear vacuoles. The nuclei are cytologically bland, round, with grooves, exhibiting minimal atypia and no mitotic activity. The tumor cells are positive for CD10, CD56, CD99, WT1, β-catenin (nuclear and cytoplasmic), and α1-antitrypsin, and they may stain for CAM5.2 (dot-like perinuclear), PR, synaptophysin, and KIT (CD117). Most tumor contain CTNNB1 mutations.
cases.discussion: Both solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of ovary and microcystic stromal tumor have CTNNB1 mutations, however, the latter lacks a pseudopapillary growth pattern or the characteristic nuclear grooves of solid pseudopapillary tumor. Adult granulosa cell tumor (AGCT) usually exhibits nuclear grooves but lacks abundant eosinophilic globules. In yolk sac tumor, eosinophilic hyaline globules may be conspicuous both within cells and in the stroma, but this tumor expresses germ cell markers.

references.text: Deshpande V, Oliva E, Young RH. Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the ovary: a report of 3 primary ovarian tumors resembling those of the pancreas. Am J Surg Pathol. 2010 Oct;34(10):1514-20.

Case presented by Dr. Deyin Xing, MD, PhD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This is a 40 year old female with a right ovarian mass. Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.histology: This ovarian mass is a microcystic stromal tumor. A majority of these stromal tumors exhibit the classic triad of microcysts, solid cellular zones, and fibrous stroma, in various proportions. On low power, the microcystic areas as well as solid cellular areas are intersected by fibrous stroma with hyaline plaques. The microcysts consist of small to large-sized oval to round cystic spaces, in areas merging into larger irregular channels. Rarely, there are variants of microcystic stromal tumors that are predominantly or entirely composed of diffuse, corded, or nested cells with absence of apparent microcysts. On high power, the tumor cells contain a moderate amount of finely granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm. Intracytoplasmic vacuoles can be identified. The nuclei are bland, round to oval with small indistinct nucleoli and a low mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry staining of the tumor cells will be positive for nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin, and positive for CD10, WT1, FOXL2, cyclin D1, and SF1, but negative for inhibin, calretinin, and EMA. Most microcystic stromal tumors have a point mutation in CTNNB1 (encoding β-catenin) or mutation in APC. These tumors can be associated with familial adenomatous polyposis.
cases.discussion: Microcystic stromal tumor has overlapping features with other sex-cord stromal tumor including adult granulosa cell tumor, fibrothecoma and steroid cell tumor. However, its distinct immuoprofile can facilitate the classification. Morphologically, even in the solid variant, focal microcysts can be seen.

references.text: Irving JA, Lee CH, Yip S, Oliva E, McCluggage WG, Young RH. Microcystic Stromal Tumor: A Distinctive Ovarian Sex Cord-Stromal Neoplasm Characterized by FOXL2, SF-1, WT-1, Cyclin D1, and beta-catenin Nuclear Expression and CTNNB1 Mutations. Am J Surg Pathol. 2015 Oct;39(10):1420-6.

cases.vignette: This is a 30 year old female with an abdominal wall mass. Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Russell Vang, MD, and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This is a 30 year old female with an abdominal wall mass. Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.histology: This is an epithelioid trophoblastic tumor that has metastasized to the abdominal wall. Epithelioid trophoblastic tumor is a malignant neoplasm of chorionic-type intermediate trophoblast. This tumor is characterized by nests or cords of round, plump, uniform cells in a fibrous sclerotic stroma with fat intermixed. There are tumor cell islands centered around vessels in a perivascular distribution. There is also notable geographic necrosis and eosinophilic hyaline-like material present in the center of tumor nests or between tumor cells. On higher power, the tumor cells have moderate amount of finely granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, distinct cell membranes, round nuclei, and small prominent nucleoli. The mitotic count will vary. The tumor cells will stain positive for HSD3B1, HLA-G, p63, cyclin E, α-inhibin, and GATA3. In some cases, a Ki-67 proliferation index of >10% is helpful for diagnosis. This patient had a past medical history of epithelioid trophoblastic tumor, consistent with the diagnosis. There is a mild to moderate elevation of serum hCG of <2500 mIU/mL that can be detected in 80% of cases. Metastasis can occur in 25-30% of cases.
cases.discussion: The differential diagnosis includes choriocarcinoma, which is another type of gestational trophoblastic disease. However, choriocarcinoma consists of three different cell types (syncytial trophoblastic cells and cytotrophoblastic cells as well as intermediate trophoblast cells) that are cells that normally form part of the placenta. Placental site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT) is also a neoplastic proliferation of implantation-type intermediate trophoblast, however, the tumor will be positive for HPL and negative for p63 negative. This contrasts with the HPL negativity and p63 positivity seen in epithelioid trophoblastic tumors. Squamous cell carcinoma is on the differential, however, it usually does not have an increase in hCG, is negative for trophoblastic differentiation markers, and has definitive cell bridges and true keratin formation, unlike epithelioid trophoblastic tumors.

references.text: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Female Genital Tumours. WHO Classification of Tumours, ( 5th ed.). IARC; 2020.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Russell Vang, MD, and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This is a 60 year old female with a left ovarian mass. Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.histology: This is a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, composed of varying proportions of Sertoli and Leydig cells intersected by fibrous or edematous connective tissue. The sertoliform tubules are bland and immature-looking and arranged in nests or cords. These Sertoli cells have poorly defined cell borders, scant cytoplasm, and small oval to round nuclei. Between the sertoliform tubules are clusters of Leydig cells, which contain abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Subtypes of Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors according to the criteria of the World Health Organization (WHO) include well-differentiated, moderately differentiated, poorly differentiated, and retiform. This case is a well-differentiated tumor, which contains Sertoli cells arranged in a tubular pattern separated by more Leydig cells and has no DICER1 mutation. The cells lining the tubules exhibit little nuclear atypia and only rare mitotic figures. However, it is more common for these tumors to be moderately or poorly differentiated. Moderately differentiated tumors consist of immature cords or islands of Sertoli cells. Well-defined tubules may be present with mature Leydig cells. Poorly differentiated tumors have sheet-like growth of spindle-shaped tumor cells resembling sarcomas. These tumors may lose immature cords of cells and exhibit cellular atypia with more mitoses. The periphery of moderately to poorly differentiated tumors may contain heterologous elements, such as skeletal muscle, cartilage, and mucinous glands. Irregular slit-like spaces and retiform patterns can be present. These moderately and poorly differentiated tumors are mostly sporadic but can occur in DICER1 syndrome.
cases.discussion: The differential diagnosis of sertoli-leydig cell tumor depends on their degree of differentiation and presence of heterologous or retiform components. Well-differentiated tumors may be confused with well-differentiated sertoliform endometrioid carcinoma as the glands and solid epithelial formations in this latter tumor might resemble the hollow and solid tubules of sertoli-leydig cell tumors. However, endometrioid carcinoma will have areas with the usual pattern of endometrioid caricnoma and presence of mucin at the apical borders of the tumor cells. CK7/EMA will stain positively, while inhibin and SF-1 will stain negatively in endometrioid carcinoma. Whereas, the converse is true for sertoli-leydig cell tumors. Granulosa cell tumor may have small foci of tubules indistinguishable from sertoli-leydig cell tumors. However, granulosa cells tend to be mature with pale, often grooved nuclei whereas Sertoli cells are commonly immature. Moreover, the presence of heterologous elements would never be encountered in granulosa cell tumors and is specific for sertoli-leydig cell tumors. Sertoli-cell tumors are solid with fibromatous stroma and lack leydig cell components seen here.

references.text: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Female Genital Tumours. WHO Classification of Tumours, ( 5th ed.). IARC; 2020.
Young RH, Scully RE. Ovarian Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors. A clinicopathological analysis of 207 cases. Am J Surg Pathol. 1985 Aug;9(8):543-69.

Case presented by Dr. Russell Vang, MD, and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This is a 30 year old female with a right ovarian mass.
Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.histology: This is a seromucinous borderline tumor, which is characterized by papillae with hierarchical branching as seen in serous tumors and mucinous cells resembling those in the endocervix. Larger papillae consist of edematous or fibrous stroma filled with acute inflammatory cells, such as neutrophils. There is absence of stromal invasion and absence of micropapillary architecture measuring >5mm, consistent with the classification as a borderline tumor. The epithelial lining of the papillae is often tufted, stratified, and cytologically bland. The glands are lined by mucinous epithelium with basal nuclei and abundant apical cytoplasm, resembling the epithelium of the endocervix. Multiple Mullerian cell types (endocervical-type mucinous cells, ciliated cells, hobnail cells, and eosinophilic cells) are admixed in the epithelium in different proportions. The epithelial cells are typically positive for CK7, PAX8, ER, and PR, and negative for WT1, CK20, and CDX2. Approximately 30% of these tumors are bilateral. These tumors have an association with endometriosis, most commonly endometriotic cysts. Other tumors that are associated with endometriosis include endometrioid carcinoma and clear cell carcinoma.
cases.discussion: Seromucinous borderline tumors have papillary architecture closely resembling serous tumors but contain endocervical-type mucinous epithelium, which is negative for WT-1. In contrast, serous borderline tumors consist of epithelial cells that are low cuboidal with not much-rich cytoplasm, and the epithelial cells would be positive for WT1. Mucinous borderline tumors would display glandular and cystic architecture rather than predominantly papillary architecture (although mucinous borderline tumors can have villous architecture), and the predominant cell-type has intestinal-type mucinous cytoplasm with presence of goblet cells or Paneth cells. Seromucinous carcinoma (considered to be variants of endometrioid carcinoma with mucinous diffferentiation in the current WHO Classification) would have more cytologic atypia and architectural complexity than seromucinous borderline tumors. Furthermore, seromucinous carcinomas may exhibit a complex cribriform growth pattern involving the surface of papillae or lining cystic spaces.

references.text: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Female Genital Tumours. WHO Classification of Tumours, ( 5th ed.). IARC; 2020.

Shappell HW, Riopel MA, Smith Sehdev AE, Ronnett BM, Kurman RJ. Diagnostic criteria and behavior of ovarian seromucinous (endocervical-type mucinous and mixed cell-type) tumors: atypical proliferative (borderline) tumors, intraepithelial, microinvasive, and invasive carcinomas. Am J Surg Pathol. 2002 Dec;26(12):1529-41.

IPMN is a cystic pancreatic neoplasm, usually in the head, that is known for its association with invasive carcinoma. Pancreatic cyst fluid analysis with ancillary molecular studies may assist in determining what type of cyst (serous, mucinous) especially if there is elevated cyst fluid CEA and GNAS mutations that may point towards a mucinous cyst.

Morphologically, IPMNs are characterized by cystic spaces with papillary projections lined by gastric-type (cells resembling gastric foveolae and sometimes with intestinal metaplasia), intestinal type (tall columnar epithelium that resembles intestinal villous adenomas), and pancreatobiliary type (complex, thin branching papillae with biliary-appearing glands and low cuboidal cells with prominent nucleoli). Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) is defined as a nontumoral form of dysplasia and would not have clinical, mass-forming manifestations (i.e., they are defined as microscopic incidental findings). They commonly arise next to areas of invasive carcinoma. Morphologically, IPMNs are characterized by cystic spaces with papillary projections lined by gastric-type (cells resembling gastric foveolae and sometimes with intestinal metaplasia), intestinal type (tall columnar epithelium that resembles intestinal villous adenomas), and pancreatobiliary type (complex, thin branching papillae with biliary-appearing glands and low cuboidal cells with prominent nucleoli).  Based on the histologic findings in the current case, this may be best classified as a gastric type IPMN without high-grade dysplasia, as the lining resembles gastric foveolae and there are no atypical mitoses nor hyperchromasia.

The background pancreas may have been obstructed due to the compression from the cystic IPMN, leading to pancreatic secretion backup and eventual lobular atrophy that is evidenced here as background chronic pancreatitis. The slit-like glands in the lobules and the increased chronic inflammation may be confused for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma; however, there is no stark variation in nuclear size (4:1 nuclear size discrepancy between adjacent glands), and the glands retain a lobular configuration.

Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) is defined as a nontumoral form of dysplasia and would not have clinical, mass-forming manifestations (i.e., they are defined as microscopic incidental findings). They commonly arise next to areas of invasive carcinoma. cases.question_text:
Presented by Lisa Rooper, MD, and prepared by Samuel Law, MD.
This is a 40-year-old female with a mandibular mass.
Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.histology: Histologic sections are composed of nests, cords, and sheets of polygonal, eosinophilic, squamoid cells with ample cytoplasm and pleomorphic nuclei in an admixed background of grungy to psammomatous calcification and amyloid-like matrix. The combination of these polygonal cells, the grungy calcification, and the amyloid-like matrix deposition is suggestive of the diagnosis of calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor.
cases.discussion:
Calcifying epithelial odontogenic tumor (CEOT), also formerly known as Pindborg tumor (after the Danish pathologist Jens Pindborg who discovered the entity in 1955) is a rare, benign neoplasm usually of the premolar and molar mandibular regions (posterior mandible). A subset of cases may also be identified in the maxilla or in the gingiva, where it is known as a peripheral tumor. About 50% of cases of CEOT are associated with an unerupted or impacted tooth. Radiologically they resemble a dentigerous cyst with lesions demonstrating lucency with varying degrees of scattered calcifications (from lucent to dense), giving a “driven snow” appearance on radiography. Histologically, CEOT is characterized by the combination of pleomorphic polyhedral squamous epithelial cells with intercellular bridging, focal psammomatous bodies, amyloid bodies comprised of degenerated keratin filaments, and basophilic calcifications and a lack of architectural pleomorphism (no whorls, or cribriform pattern). The clear cell variant may demonstrate clear, vacuolated cytoplasm. The amyloid component may react with Congo red stain.

The lesion occurs in patients of the 4th to 5th decade and may be invasive and exhibit local recurrence status post resection, but prognostically it is less aggressive than ameloblastoma.

Ademonatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) usually occurs in females below the age of 20 years with a propensity for an impacted tooth in the anterior maxilla. Histologically it would demonstrate nodular, squamoid islands and cribriform architecture surrounded by a thick fibrous capsule. Adenoid ameloblastoma can also be associated with impacted teeth, but histologically they demonstrate extensive dentinoid clear cells with occasional ghost cells arranged in morules and whorls like AOT that is not typical of CEOT. Lastly, dentigerous cysts are another entity associated with unerupted teeth, but radiographically are fluid-filled lesions that encase the crown of the unerupted tooth of individuals in the 3rd and 4th decades. Histologically it is composed of inflamed stratified squamous epithelium without basal palisading.

cases.vignette: This is a 50-year-old male with a nasal mass. Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.question_text:
Presented by Lisa Rooper, MD, and prepared by Samuel Law, MD.
This is a 50-year-old male with a nasal mass.
Select the correct diagnosis.
cases.histology: Histologic sections are composed of pieces of tumor with exuberant chronic inflammation and areas of cribriform glands and squamous pearl formation, with scattered areas demonstrating basaloid morphology. This case was positive upon HPV in-situ-hybridization immunohistochemistry. The IHC findings and the combined presence of cribriform glands and squamous differentiation points to a diagnosis of HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma.
cases.discussion:
HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma is a neoplasm described as recently as 2013 that is located exclusively in the sinonasal tract and is noted for its strong association with human papillomavirus 33 (HPV33) and its negativity for MYB/NFIB translocations. This tumor was formerly known as HPV-related sinonasal carcinoma with adenoid cystic carcinoma-like features. It is noted for its wide age range, and high risk HPV is detected in all reported cases, with HPV 33 detected in 68% [Head Neck Pathol 2018 Sep 26]. The usual histologic features include areas that resemble ACC with tubular, cribriform, and solid patterns, as evidenced by biphasic ductal and myoepithelial differentiation, as well as squamous and basaloid differentiation. Rarely, sarcomatoid areas with staghorn vasculature or heterologous mesenchymal elements may be present.

Based on the curated cases in the literature, this neoplasm is associated with high frequency of late local recurrence decades after initial surgery but distant metastases are rare. Current treatment revolves around surgical resection with negative margins and sometimes radiation therapy.

Though ACC shares morphologic overlap with HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma, ACC would not be positive for high-risk HPV in-situ hybridization and has no known association with HPV infection. ACC would also have a MYB/NFIB translocation in most cases. Sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma would be characterized by predominantly squamous differentiation and no biphasic morphology nor myoepithelial differentiation. Lastly, SMARCB1 deficient sinonasal carcinoma would demonstrate INI1/BAF47 (SMARCB1) loss by immunohistochemistry, and it will be HPV-ISH negative.

Correct answer: HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma

Histology:

Histologic sections are composed of pieces of tumor with exuberant chronic inflammation and areas of cribriform glands and squamous pearl formation, with scattered areas demonstrating basaloid morphology. This case was positive upon HPV in-situ-hybridization immunohistochemistry. The IHC findings and the combined presence of cribriform glands and squamous differentiation points to a diagnosis of HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma.

Discussion:

HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma is a neoplasm described as recently as 2013 that is located exclusively in the sinonasal tract and is noted for its strong association with human papillomavirus 33 (HPV33) and its negativity for MYB/NFIB translocations. This tumor was formerly known as HPV-related sinonasal carcinoma with adenoid cystic carcinoma-like features. It is noted for its wide age range, and high risk HPV is detected in all reported cases, with HPV 33 detected in 68% [Head Neck Pathol 2018 Sep 26]. The usual histologic features include areas that resemble ACC with tubular, cribriform, and solid patterns, as evidenced by biphasic ductal and myoepithelial differentiation, as well as squamous and basaloid differentiation. Rarely, sarcomatoid areas with staghorn vasculature or heterologous mesenchymal elements may be present.

Based on the curated cases in the literature, this neoplasm is associated with high frequency of late local recurrence decades after initial surgery but distant metastases are rare. Current treatment revolves around surgical resection with negative margins and sometimes radiation therapy.

Though ACC shares morphologic overlap with HPV-related multiphenotypic sinonasal carcinoma, ACC would not be positive for high-risk HPV in-situ hybridization and has no known association with HPV infection. ACC would also have a MYB/NFIB translocation in most cases. Sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma would be characterized by predominantly squamous differentiation and no biphasic morphology nor myoepithelial differentiation. Lastly, SMARCB1 deficient sinonasal carcinoma would demonstrate INI1/BAF47 (SMARCB1) loss by immunohistochemistry, and it will be HPV-ISH negative.
